questions.prompt: What is Chapter 9's main claim about authenticity?
choices: It matters because a self-owned message is often more persuasive than imitation
It matters because good speakers should refuse all outside influence
It matters because authenticity replaces the need for preparation

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the audience trusts a message more when it sounds like it belongs to the speaker.
explanation.direct: Gallo treats originality as part of credibility rather than as a decorative personal preference.
explanation.competitive: Ownership is the advantage. Isolation is not.

questions.prompt: How does Gallo mainly frame enthusiasm in this chapter?
choices: As generic animation that all speakers should imitate
As real commitment that changes audience response when it feels genuine
As a replacement for clear structure

explanation.gentle: Enthusiasm helps most when the audience can feel that the speaker truly cares.
explanation.direct: The chapter links energy to persuasion only when that energy grows out of genuine belief.
explanation.competitive: Real concern carries weight. Performance by itself does not.

questions.prompt: Harper's product update sounds like a copied keynote. Which response best fits the chapter?
choices: Keep the borrowed style because famous delivery patterns create automatic trust
Rewrite the talk so it keeps the useful structure but sounds like Harper's real expertise and voice
Remove all preparation so the talk feels more raw and therefore more authentic

explanation.gentle: Harper should keep the useful method but make the message sound more like her own real voice.
explanation.direct: The chapter favors self-owned delivery over polished imitation, not chaos over preparation.
explanation.competitive: Take the tools, drop the impersonation.

questions.prompt: What is Ms. Voss asking Micah to do in Northgate seminar room?
choices: Copy the famous speaker more accurately so the model becomes clearer
Stop using any learned speaking method at all
Separate useful technique from borrowed identity and rebuild the speech in his own voice

explanation.gentle: Micah should keep the useful method but remove the copied mannerisms.
explanation.direct: The repair is to adapt the technique without imitating the speaker's identity.
explanation.competitive: Learn from the model. Do not become the model.

questions.prompt: Which trap does Chapter 9 most clearly warn against?
choices: Assuming authenticity means never revising a talk
Assuming a polished borrowed style is just as persuasive as a self-owned one
Assuming speakers should stay inside one topic forever

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that imitation can weaken trust even when the talk sounds smooth.
explanation.direct: Borrowed polish may impress at first, but it can still damage credibility when the audience senses a mismatch.

questions.prompt: What makes a chapter-faithful version of authenticity?
choices: Skipping structure so the talk feels more natural
Using craft and preparation while still sounding rooted in your own expertise and conviction
Copying successful emotion while changing only the wording

explanation.gentle: The chapter does not reject preparation. It asks the speaker to keep the finished talk believable and self-owned.
explanation.direct: Authenticity here means crafted delivery that still sounds connected to the real speaker.
explanation.competitive: The goal is owned craft, not raw mess or polished imitation.

questions.prompt: Sonia is choosing between sounding impressive and sounding believable. Which choice best fits the chapter?
choices: Use the version that sounds more honestly connected to her real concern
Keep the more borrowed register because audiences always trust prestige language more
Remove all rhetorical choices so the appeal sounds completely casual

explanation.gentle: Sonia should choose the version the audience can believe belongs to her.
explanation.direct: The chapter values credibility rooted in real conviction over borrowed impressiveness.

questions.prompt: Why does Trent's polished presentation still underperform?
choices: Because polished talks always feel less human than rough ones
Because the room sensed strong preparation but not enough ownership behind the voice
Because work presentations should avoid confident delivery

explanation.gentle: Trent's talk sounded prepared, but the audience felt that the voice did not fully belong to him.
explanation.direct: This is the chapter's secondhand-voice problem. Mechanics were present, but credibility weakened.
explanation.competitive: The surface looked professional. The signal still sounded rented.

questions.prompt: Camille copies a famous speaker's full delivery package in Riverton speech lab. What does that reveal?
choices: Imitation can win attention early and still weaken trust later
School speakers should never study strong presenters
Audience trust depends mainly on exact pauses and gestures

explanation.gentle: Copied polish may look strong at first but still feel less believable later.
explanation.direct: Camille's result shows why the chapter separates learning technique from borrowing identity.
explanation.competitive: Attention can rise before credibility sends the bill.

questions.prompt: Why is authenticity the right closing discipline for the book?
choices: Because authenticity makes every earlier tool unnecessary
Because all the earlier tools work better when a believable speaker is carrying them
Because the book's final lesson is to ignore every outside model completely

explanation.gentle: The book ends here because the audience has to believe the speaker behind all the earlier techniques.
explanation.direct: Chapter 9 turns authenticity into a capstone by showing that credibility affects every earlier tool in the system.
explanation.competitive: The tools still matter, but they hit harder when the room trusts the person using them.
